findings.description: The inline user policy grants wildcard actions (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) on Resource "*", allowing the service user to read/modify any bucket, launch or terminate any instance, and deploy arbitrary Lambda code. Compromise of this user's credentials leads to broad account takeover, and ec2/lambda wildcards enable privilege escalation via iam:PassRole-adjacent workflows.

A permanent IAM access key is created for the service user and its secret is stored in Terraform state in plaintext (no pgp_key is supplied, so the secret attribute is unencrypted in state). Long-lived static keys attached to a highly privileged user are a prime credential-leak target and there is no rotation mechanism.

No pgp_key argument is set, so encrypted_secret will be null and the raw secret access key is only available as the plaintext `secret` attribute persisted in Terraform state, exposing credentials to anyone with state file access.

The `svc_deploy_key_material` output exports access key material from the access key resource. Outputs are stored unencrypted in Terraform state and printed to the console/CI logs, leaking credentials for a user with account-wide ec2/s3/lambda privileges. The output is also not marked sensitive.

A static IAM user with attached long-lived keys is used for deployment rather than an assumable IAM role with temporary STS credentials, and force_destroy = true allows silent removal of keys/policies. This maximizes the blast radius of any credential leak and removes MFA/session-scoped controls.
